analysis.one_liner: Bans grossly excessive price increases and lets the FTC penalize large sellers that gouge during emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill has not moved since its July 2025 introduction: 20 cosponsors, all Democrats, two House committees, and no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime-like violation for any seller, anywhere in a supply chain, to charge a "grossly excessive price" for a good or service. During declared emergencies and other market shocks, big companies with $1 billion or more in U.S. revenue would be presumed to be price gouging if they charge far more than their pre-shock prices, and they would have to prove the increase came from costs beyond their control. The Federal Trade Commission could sue violators and seek penalties of up to 5% of a company's annual revenue, state attorneys general could do the same for their residents, and public companies would have to disclose their margins and pricing decisions in securities filings during a shock.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who face sudden price spikes on essentials during hurricanes, pandemics, power outages, or supply disruptions. Anyone harmed by a violation could get restitution through FTC or state attorney general suits, and the disclosure requirements would show the public exactly how big companies' prices and margins moved during a crisis.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers hit by crisis price spikes

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any seller, regardless of its position in the supply chain, to sell a good or service at a "grossly excessive price" — no federal law currently imposes a general price-gouging ban.

During an "exceptional market shock" — a hurricane, public health emergency, war, energy shortage, or a President-declared major disaster — a company with at least $1 billion in U.S. revenue that charges a price far above its own pre-shock average or competitors' prices is presumed to be violating the law, and can escape only by proving by clear and convincing evidence the increase came from costs outside its control.

Gives the FTC independent authority to sue in federal court to stop violations, obtain civil penalties of up to 5% of the violator's parent company's annual revenue, and win damages, restitution, or other compensation for aggrieved consumers.
Lets state attorneys general bring the same claims on behalf of their residents in federal or state court, and expressly preserves stronger state price-gouging laws rather than preempting them.

Requires public companies to disclose in their quarterly and annual securities filings, for any quarter with a market shock, their price and volume changes, gross margins by product category, how much of revenue growth came from price versus volume, and a narrative explanation of their pricing strategy.

analysis.who_pays: Large companies — especially big retailers, grocery chains, and energy and consumer goods sellers with $1 billion or more in U.S. revenue — would face fines up to 5% of parent-company revenue, litigation exposure, and new disclosure duties. Taxpayers would fund a $1 billion appropriation for the FTC to enforce the law. Companies would bear the cost of compiling margin and pricing data, some of which could show up in prices.

drawbacks.text: The central standard — "grossly excessive price" — is left for the FTC to define after enactment; the bill only directs the Commission to consider whether prices at or above 120% of the prior six-month market average should count, leaving companies and courts to guess what conduct becomes illegal.

The emergency presumption and steepest penalties apply only to large firms: companies whose parent earned under $100 million in U.S. revenue are exempt if they show their price increases track their own costs, creating a two-tier system in which identical conduct is treated differently based on company size.

A company hit with the emergency presumption must rebut it with clear and convincing evidence — a high bar — that its price increase came entirely from costs beyond its control, which critics would argue could deter legitimate price increases during real supply shortages.
The bill appropriates $1 billion to the FTC, available until 2033, as new federal spending on enforcement and rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real, recurring consumer harm — price spikes on essentials during emergencies — and gives both federal and state enforcers tools to return money to consumers. The costs are real too: a vague core standard that the FTC must define after enactment, a size-based carve-out that exempts most small businesses, a high evidentiary bar for companies that do get accused, and a $1 billion enforcement appropriation. Whether the deterrence is worth the litigation uncertainty depends largely on how the FTC writes the rules, which the bill largely delegates. As a response to emergency gouging it is aggressive but not reckless; its breadth beyond emergencies (a general ban on grossly excessive prices at all times) is the part most open to challenge.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2025 and sent to two House committees, and neither has taken it up since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the Price Gouging Prevention Act of 2025 on July 17, 2025.
The same day, the Speaker's referral sent it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Financial Services Committee for the portions under each committee's jurisdiction.
Twenty House Democrats — all of the bill's cosponsors — signed on; no Republican has cosponsored it.
The bill's full action history shows no further activity after the committee referral: no hearings, no markups, no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change behavior: there is still no federal price-gouging law, so large sellers of goods and services continue operating under the pre-existing rules with no federal penalties for excessive pricing and no new public disclosure of crisis-era margins. Consumers are no worse off than before, but the protections the bill promised are not in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large sellers; no new pricing rules took effect

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican has signed on, and with no votes taken the partisan split is only apparent, not tested.

industries.industry: Large retailers, grocers, and consumer goods sellers
industries.note: These firms would face federal penalties of up to 5% of parent-company revenue for grossly excessive prices, with a presumption of violation during emergencies, and public disclosure of their margins and pricing strategy. The bill targets precisely the practice — raising prices on captive customers during a shock — from which these firms profit, so their interest runs against consumers here.

Energy price spikes after outages and disasters are a classic price-gouging scenario the bill's 'exceptional market shock' definition expressly covers, including power failures and energy shortages. Energy sellers would face the same presumption and penalties as other large firms.

Issuers filing Form 10-Q or 10-K after a shock quarter would have to publish tabulated margin, cost, and price data plus a narrative of their pricing decisions. The burden falls on the companies; the benefit is information for investors and the public, which is why the industry's interest in avoiding it runs against transparency.

analysis.trajectory: A newly introduced House bill with no Republican cosponsors, parked in two committees, rarely reaches the floor in this Congress. Barring a decision by the Energy and Commerce or Financial Services chairs to hold a markup, or the price-gouging language being attached to a larger package, the bill is likely to sit without action until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
